short_description: Filamentous green mould built from septate hyaline hyphae. Erect conidiophores branch into metulae and flask-shaped phialides that pinch off unbranched chains of green conidia - the little brush (penicillus) that names the genus. It secretes penicillin to keep competing bacteria at a distance, and Alexander Fleming's accidental sighting of that bacteria-free zone in 1928 became the first antibiotic.
colour_note: Genuinely pigmented, unlike most microbes in this atlas: the CONIDIA carry a blue-green to grey-green pigment, so a mature colony is velvety blue-green with a white growing margin, and P. chrysogenum also exudes a bright yellow soluble pigment into the agar (chrysogenum = 'golden-producing'). The hyphae, conidiophore, metulae and phialides themselves are HYALINE - colourless and translucent. House palette across all styles: hyphae/conidiophore pale translucent ivory with a thin dusty-ochre wall line, septa a slightly darker teal-grey cross-line, metulae pale sage, phialides warm cream, conidia sage/blue-green spheres (palest at the base of each chain, where the youngest sit), background neutral dark charcoal (aged paper for watercolor).

reference.caveat: Identified to genus (Penicillium sp., lactophenol cotton blue tease mount) rather than sequenced to species. It shows exactly the diagnostic brush architecture of P. chrysogenum - stipe branching into metulae and phialides with unbranched conidial chains, and no swollen Aspergillus vesicle - but the species identity is not independently confirmed.
